title: After the Acropolis: the Ancient Agora or the National Archaeological Museum?
subtitle: One is ten minutes downhill, the other two kilometres north. What each holds, how long it takes, what the tickets include.
excerpt: With one afternoon left in Athens after the Acropolis, the choice is between the Ancient Agora at the foot of the rock and the National Archaeological Museum. What to see in each, how long to allow, and what the tickets cover.

meta_title: Athens: the Ancient Agora or the Archaeological Museum?
meta_description: After the Acropolis: the Ancient Agora or the National Archaeological Museum. What each holds, how long to allow, and what the tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The Temple of Hephaestus above the trees of the Ancient Agora in Athens

content_html:
[place attraction="ancient-agora-of-athens" city="athens"]

In the months before the German army reached Athens in April 1941, the staff of the National Archaeological Museum emptied their own building. They dug trenches under the floors of the galleries, laid the marble statues in them and covered them with sand. The bronzes went into crates, the gold into the vaults of the Bank of Greece. When the occupiers arrived, they were shown bare rooms.

Everything came back up after the war, and it took years to put on show again. That collection is one of two things most visitors to Athens miss, because they have a morning on the Acropolis and an afternoon left. The other lies at the foot of the rock: the Ancient Agora, where the city did its daily business. If you have time for only one, this is how to choose.

The short answer

Choose the Agora if you want to stay outdoors, walk among ruins and see a Greek temple that still has its roof. It is ten minutes downhill from the Acropolis and takes an hour and a half. Choose the museum if you want the objects: the gold of Mycenae, the great bronzes pulled from the sea, the painted walls of Santorini. It is indoors, cool in summer, and needs two hours plus the trip to reach it.

With a full day, do the Acropolis first, the Agora straight after, and the museum in the afternoon or the next morning.

The Ancient Agora: what you are looking at

The agora was the open square of ancient Athens: market, law courts, council house, and the place where Socrates talked to whoever would stop. Until 1931 a whole neighbourhood stood on top of it. The American School of Classical Studies bought and took down several hundred houses to excavate, and its work here continues.

Three things deserve your time:

  • The Temple of Hephaestus, on the low hill at the west side. Built in the second half of the 5th century BC, in the same decades as the Parthenon, it is the best preserved Doric temple in Greece. It survived because it was used as a church until 1834.
  • The Stoa of Attalos, the long two-storey colonnade on the east side. The original was a gift from Attalos II, king of Pergamon, around 150 BC. What you see was rebuilt on the old foundations from 1953 to 1956.
  • The museum inside the stoa, small and easy to underrate: the pottery shards on which Athenians scratched the name of the man they wanted exiled, a marble allotment machine used to pick jurors by lot, and a Spartan shield taken as a trophy in 425 BC.

The ground floor of the Stoa of Attalos, rebuilt in the 1950s. The site museum is behind the wall on the right. Photo: Erik Drost, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Between temple and stoa runs the Panathenaic Way, the road the great procession took up to the Acropolis. Beside it stands the small Byzantine church of the Holy Apostles, about a thousand years old. There is little shade away from the stoa and the temple hill, so carry water.

A path through the Agora, with the Acropolis above it. Photo: Zde, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The National Archaeological Museum: what you are looking at

The museum is a long neoclassical building on Patission Street, finished in 1889, about two kilometres north of the Agora. The nearest metro stations are Omonia and Victoria, each around ten minutes away on foot. Do not try to see it all. These are the things that justify the journey:

  • Mycenae, straight ahead from the entrance: the gold death masks that Heinrich Schliemann dug out of the shaft graves in 1876, including the one he named for Agamemnon. It is some three centuries older than any Trojan War could have been.
  • The Artemision bronze: a bearded god over two metres tall, arm drawn back to throw, cast about 460 BC and found in the sea off Cape Artemision in the 1920s. Whether he held a thunderbolt (Zeus) or a trident (Poseidon) is still argued.
  • The Jockey of Artemision: a small boy on a galloping horse, from the same wreck, made some three hundred years later.
  • The Antikythera finds: a bronze youth and the corroded gearwheels of the Antikythera mechanism, a device for following the sun, the moon and the calendar, from a shipwreck found by sponge divers in 1900.
  • The frescoes from Akrotiri, upstairs: two boys boxing, and a room of swallows and lilies, from the town on Santorini that a volcanic eruption buried in the Bronze Age.

The gold mask from Mycenae that Schliemann named for Agamemnon. Photo: Jebulon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The Artemision bronze in its hall: Zeus or Poseidon, about to throw. Photo: George E. Koronaios, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

What the tickets include

An Acropolis ticket does not open either place. Each has its own ticket and its own desk. What our partner sells falls into three kinds:

  • A ticket with an audio tour: entry booked ahead, plus a commentary in the partner's app on your own phone, with a map from stop to stop. The one for the Agora lists entry to the site and to the museum in the stoa.
  • An entrance ticket alone, for the Archaeological Museum. Read the options when you book: some of them name an audio guide, while the listing says the partner's own tour is not part of it.
  • An audio tour without a ticket, for either place. It is the commentary only. You still buy your entry, ahead or at the gate.

Bring earphones for any of them, and download the tour before you leave the hotel. One caution: a title and its contents can differ, so read the list of what is included and check that the entry named is for the place you mean. The Acropolis Museum, the modern building below the south side of the rock, is a third place, with a ticket of its own.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for the Agora and the Archaeological Museum, with today's prices:

[partner city="athens" match="agora,archaeological" limit="5"]

When to go, and in what order

The Agora is an open site and closes earlier in winter than in summer. In the hot months only the first hours of the morning and the last of the afternoon are comfortable. The usual order works: the Acropolis at opening time, then down the north-west side of the rock to the Agora, then lunch. Keep the museum for the heat of the afternoon.

State sites and museums in Greece have long been free on a few fixed days of the year and on the first Sunday of the winter months, which fills them. Hours for both places change with the season: the current ones are on our pages for the Ancient Agora and the National Archaeological Museum.

From here

From the Agora's gate on Adrianou Street you are five minutes from Monastiraki Square and the lanes of Plaka. The Roman Agora, with the Tower of the Winds, is a short walk east. From the museum, the metro at Omonia takes you back to the centre in two stops. For the rest of Athens, or to fit it into a longer trip, open the trip planner for Greece.

Cover photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: Does the Acropolis ticket include the Ancient Agora?
faqs.a: No. The Ancient Agora has its own ticket, which also covers the small museum inside the Stoa of Attalos. The National Archaeological Museum is ticketed separately too.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Ancient Agora?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half: the Temple of Hephaestus, the Stoa of Attalos with its museum, and the walk between them along the Panathenaic Way.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens?
faqs.a: Two hours are enough for the Mycenaean gold, the Artemision bronzes, the Antikythera finds and the frescoes from Akrotiri. Add the trip: the museum is about two kilometres north of the Acropolis area.

faqs.q: Where is the Mask of Agamemnon?
faqs.a: In the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, in the Mycenaean hall straight ahead from the entrance. It was found at Mycenae in 1876.

faqs.q: Is the Acropolis Museum the same as the National Archaeological Museum?
faqs.a: No. The Acropolis Museum is the modern building below the south side of the rock and shows what was found on the Acropolis. The National Archaeological Museum is a separate, older museum two kilometres to the north, with finds from all of Greece.

title: Plaka, Anafiotika and Monastiraki on foot: a two-hour route, and what is free along it
subtitle: From Syntagma to Monastiraki around the foot of the Acropolis, stop by stop, with the places that ask for a ticket.
excerpt: A two-hour walk through the old town of Athens, from Syntagma Square through Plaka and the island lanes of Anafiotika to Monastiraki, with what is free on the way, what needs a ticket and what an audio walk adds.
longtail_phrases: how to walk from Syntagma to Monastiraki through Plaka
how do you get to Anafiotika
is Plaka free to visit
when is the changing of the guard in Athens
can you see the Tower of the Winds without a ticket
meta_title: Plaka, Anafiotika, Monastiraki: a two-hour walk
meta_description: A two-hour walk from Syntagma through Plaka and Anafiotika to Monastiraki: the stops in order, what is free, what needs a ticket, what an audio walk adds.

featured_image.alt: The roofs of Athens and Mount Lycabettus seen from the lanes of Anafiotika

content_html:
[place attraction="tower-of-the-winds" city="athens"]

When Athens became the capital of the new Greek kingdom in 1834, it was a small town, and it needed a palace. Builders were brought in from the islands, among them stonemasons from Anafi, a speck of land east of Santorini. They needed somewhere to live, and land in the growing capital was already dear.

So they built on the one slope nobody was meant to build on: the rock directly under the Acropolis. The story told in Athens is that they relied on an old custom, by which a house roofed between sunset and sunrise could not be pulled down. What they put up looks like what they had left: white cubes, flat roofs, lanes one person wide. A few dozen houses survive. The quarter is called Anafiotika, little Anafi, and it is the best reason to walk through the old town below the rock instead of taking the metro past it.

The route in brief

The walk runs from Syntagma Square to Monastiraki Square, around the east and north sides of the Acropolis. It is about three kilometres and takes two hours with stops, more if you go into the ticketed sites. Most of it is on streets closed to traffic. The one climb is the stepped lanes up to Anafiotika, which are uneven and narrow: wear shoes that grip, and do not bring a pushchair. In summer, start before nine or after five.

Stop by stop

1. Syntagma Square

The palace those masons worked on is the plain building at the top of the square, now the Greek Parliament. In front of it two soldiers of the presidential guard, the Evzones, stand at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. They change on the hour, with a fuller ceremony on Sunday mornings. Watching is free.

2. The cathedral and the church beside it

Walk down Mitropoleos Street to the Metropolitan Cathedral, finished in 1862. The building to look at is the small one in its shadow: the Little Metropolis, a medieval church whose walls are a collage of older carved stones, ancient and Byzantine, among them a frieze showing the months of the year.

3. The Monument of Lysicrates

Turn south into Plaka along Adrianou and Kydathineon streets, to a small round monument in a square. Lysicrates paid for a chorus that won the theatre contest of 334 BC, and put this up to carry his bronze prize. Its columns are among the oldest Corinthian columns on the outside of any building. It later stood inside a Capuchin monastery, where Lord Byron lodged in 1810 and 1811.

The Monument of Lysicrates in its square in Plaka. Photo: George E. Koronaios, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

4. Anafiotika

From the monument, go uphill towards the rock until the paving turns to whitewashed steps. There are no signs and no single path. Keep the cliff above you on your left and you come out on the north side, with the whole city below and Mount Lycabettus opposite. People live here: keep your voice down and stay out of the yards.

A lane in Anafiotika: whitewash, bougainvillea, room for one person. Photo: Zde, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

5. The Roman Agora and the Tower of the Winds

The lanes drop you beside a fenced field of columns: the market the Romans built when the old agora had filled with monuments. At its edge stands an eight-sided marble tower, each face carved with the wind that blows from that direction. Andronikos of Kyrrhos built it more than two thousand years ago as a public clock, with sundials outside and a water clock within. You see nearly all of it from the street.

The top of the Tower of the Winds. Each face carries the wind that blows from its side. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

6. Hadrian's Library and Monastiraki

Two streets north, a row of tall Corinthian columns is the front wall of the library the emperor Hadrian gave Athens in AD 132. It faces Monastiraki Square: a small Byzantine church set below the level of the paving, an 18th century mosque, the metro, the street of the flea market, and the Acropolis above the rooftops.

Monastiraki Square, with the small church of the Pantanassa in the middle. Photo: Radosław Botev, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0 PL.

What is free and what needs a ticket

Free: everything on the street. The guard, both churches, the Monument of Lysicrates, Anafiotika, the squares, and a good view of the Tower of the Winds and of Hadrian's Library through their railings.

Ticketed: going inside the Roman Agora and Hadrian's Library, each with its own ticket, and the small museums of Plaka. An Acropolis ticket is for the rock and its slopes. If you plan to add the Ancient Agora, five minutes west of Monastiraki, that is a separate ticket again.

Audio walks: what they are

Our partner sells this kind of walk as a self-guided audio tour. You pay once, download it in the partner's app, and your phone tells the stories at each stop, with a map. Nobody meets you. You start when you like and pause for coffee when you like. Bring earphones.

  • City walks. One runs from Syntagma to Monastiraki through Plaka and Anafiotika in about an hour and a half, close to the route above. Others are longer and reach the hills west of the Acropolis. None includes entry to anything.
  • A walk with an Acropolis ticket. One product pairs a city walk with an entry ticket to the Acropolis. It is the only one here that gets you through a gate.
  • A food walk. An hour around Monastiraki and Plaka on what Athenians eat and where. It is commentary: what you eat is on your own bill.

Some walks have the Acropolis in their title and do not include its ticket. Read the list of what is included before you pay.

These are the audio walks our partner sells in the centre of Athens, with today's prices:

[partner city="athens" match="pathways,cradle,charms,culinary,city" limit="5"]

When to walk it

Early morning belongs to the residents and the cats: the lanes of Anafiotika are empty and the light on the white walls is soft. By eleven the tour groups have come down from the Acropolis into Plaka. Late afternoon is the second good window, and the route then ends in Monastiraki as the square fills for the evening. At midday in July and August the climb is hard work, and there is no water on the slope.

From here

Monastiraki is a junction: one metro line runs to the port of Piraeus, another to the airport. The flea market street starts at the corner of the square, and the Ancient Agora is five minutes beyond it. For a longer look at the Tower of the Winds, go back in the morning when the Roman Agora is quiet. For the rest of Athens, open the trip planner for Greece.

Cover photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk from Syntagma to Monastiraki through Plaka?
faqs.a: About two hours with stops, over roughly three kilometres, if you go by the cathedral, the Monument of Lysicrates, Anafiotika and the Roman Agora. The direct way along Ermou Street takes ten minutes and shows you none of it.

faqs.q: How do you get to Anafiotika?
faqs.a: From the Monument of Lysicrates in Plaka, walk uphill towards the Acropolis until the street becomes whitewashed steps. There are no signs. Keep the cliff on your left and you come out on the north side of the rock.

faqs.q: Is Plaka free to visit?
faqs.a: Yes. Plaka and Anafiotika are neighbourhoods, open at all hours. Only the fenced archaeological sites, such as the Roman Agora and Hadrian's Library, and the museums ask for a ticket.

faqs.q: When is the changing of the guard in Athens?
faqs.a: The Evzones in front of the Parliament on Syntagma Square change on the hour, day and night. A fuller ceremony takes place on Sunday mornings.

faqs.q: Can you see the Tower of the Winds without a ticket?
faqs.a: You see nearly all of it from the street, through the railings of the Roman Agora. A ticket lets you walk around it and look inside.

title: Rhodes Old Town: what is free, what needs a ticket, and is the Grand Master's Palace worth it?
subtitle: The medieval town of the Knights is mostly streets, gates and a moat you walk for nothing. Four places ask for a ticket.
excerpt: What you can see for free in the medieval Old Town of Rhodes, which places need a ticket, whether the Palace of the Grand Master is worth the entry, and how Lindos fits into the same trip.

secondary_keywords: Palace of the Grand Master Rhodes worth it

featured_image.alt: The cobbled Street of the Knights in the Old Town of Rhodes, between stone buildings with arched doorways

content_html:
[place attraction="medieval-city-of-rhodes" city="rhodes"]

In 1856 lightning struck the old church of the Knights of St John at the top of the town of Rhodes. Gunpowder had been stored in the vaults beneath it and forgotten. The explosion destroyed the church, killed hundreds of people and brought down most of what was left of the building next door: the palace of the Grand Masters, who had ruled the island from 1309 to 1522.

The palace you pay to enter today was built on those ruins between 1937 and 1940, when Rhodes belonged to Italy, as a residence for the governor and a showpiece for the regime. Its floors are ancient mosaics, lifted from the island of Kos. None of this makes it less worth seeing, but it changes the question. In Rhodes the truly medieval things are mostly in the street, and free.

The town in one paragraph

The Knights Hospitaller, driven out of the Holy Land, took Rhodes in 1309 and spent two centuries fortifying it. The north of the town was theirs, with the palace, the hospital and the inns of the order. The south was the town of everyone else. In 1522 Suleiman the Magnificent besieged it for six months. The knights sailed away on the first day of 1523 and later settled on Malta. The Ottomans stayed until 1912, the Italians until the Second World War, and the island has been Greek since 1947. People still live inside the walls, which is why there is no gate to pay at.

What is free

  • The walls and the moat. About four kilometres of wall ring the town. The dry moat between the lines of defence is a public walk for much of the circuit, with stone cannonballs still lying in heaps.
  • The gates. The d'Amboise Gate of 1512, on the west side, takes you over a bridge and through a bend between two fat towers. The Marine Gate faces the harbour.
  • The Street of the Knights. A straight cobbled street climbing from the hospital to the palace, lined with the inns of the "tongues", the national groups the order was divided into. Look for the coats of arms above the doors. Before nine in the morning it is empty.
  • The lower town. Hippocrates Square with its fountain, the bazaar street of Sokratous, the Mosque of Suleiman from outside, and the Square of the Jewish Martyrs, which remembers the community deported in July 1944.

The dry moat of the Old Town, a public walk between two lines of wall. Photo: Jorge Láscar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What needs a ticket

  • The Palace of the Grand Master. The courtyard, the great staircase, the upper halls with their mosaics, and two exhibitions on ancient and medieval Rhodes on the ground floor. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.
  • The Archaeological Museum, at the foot of the Street of the Knights. It fills the knights' hospital of the 15th century, and the building, with its courtyard and its long ward upstairs, is as much the exhibit as the statues.
  • The walk on top of the walls. A stretch of the ramparts opens to visitors at limited times, with a ticket of its own. Ask at the palace, where the walk starts.
  • The Kahal Shalom Synagogue, of 1577, the oldest in Greece, with a small museum beside it. It opens to visitors in season and asks for a contribution.

The gate of the Grand Master's Palace, between its two round towers. Photo: Julian Lupyan, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Is the palace worth it?

The gate and the outer walls, the most photographed part, you see without paying. Inside, you are in a 1930s idea of a medieval palace, furnished with real ancient floors and with two good exhibitions. It is worth an hour if you like mosaics, if you want the story of the knights told in one place, or if it is noon in August and you need thick walls around you.

If you have time and money for one interior only, the Archaeological Museum gives you the more authentic building. If you plan to see both, ask at the first desk whether a combined ticket is on offer that day.

The courtyard of the palace, as rebuilt in the late 1930s. Photo: Julian Lupyan, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Lindos, the other ticket

The second great site of the island is about fifty kilometres down the east coast, an hour or more by bus from Rhodes town. Above a white village, a rock stands more than a hundred metres over the sea. On top, inside a castle of the knights, are the columns of a Hellenistic stoa, a monumental staircase and the small Temple of Athena Lindia.

The way up is on foot, a quarter of an hour of polished stone steps with no shade. Go at opening time or in the last hours of the afternoon. At the bottom of the final stair, look for the ship carved into the rock face more than two thousand years ago.

Lindos from the sea: the castle walls on the rock, the white village below. Photo: Ввласенко, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What our partner sells

  • An entry ticket to the palace with a digital guide. Entry booked ahead, with a guide on your phone. The listing gives little detail, so check what it names before you pay.
  • An entry ticket to the Acropolis of Lindos with a digital guide. Entry to the site. Nothing in the listing mentions transport: getting to Lindos is your own affair.
  • An audio tour of the Old Town. About two hours, starting at the d'Amboise Gate, in the partner's app. No entry to anything.
  • An audio walk through the Jewish quarter. About two hours, starting by the palace. Tickets along the way are not included.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells in Rhodes, with today's prices:

[partner city="rhodes" match="rhodes,lindos" limit="4"]

When to go

Rhodes is a cruise port. From mid-morning to mid-afternoon in season the main streets of the Old Town are packed, and the palace with them. Walk the Street of the Knights and the moat early, keep the interiors for the last two hours before closing, and come back after dark, when the day visitors have gone. Hours shorten in winter: the current ones are on our page for the Palace of the Grand Master.

From here

Outside the walls to the north, Mandraki harbour has its three windmills and the two bronze deer on columns at the entrance. To the west, a half-hour walk uphill, the ancient acropolis of Rhodes has a stadium and the columns of a temple of Apollo, open and free. For more on the medieval town, the Acropolis of Lindos and the rest of Rhodes, or to fit the island into a longer trip, open the trip planner for Greece.

Cover photo: Julian Lupyan, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

faqs.q: Is Rhodes Old Town free to enter?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a lived-in town and its gates are open at all hours. The streets, the Street of the Knights, the gates and the moat cost nothing. Only a few places inside ask for a ticket.

faqs.q: Is the Palace of the Grand Master in Rhodes worth it?
faqs.a: It is worth an hour for its ancient mosaic floors and its exhibitions on the history of Rhodes. Know that most of the building is a reconstruction of 1937 to 1940. The gate and outer walls can be seen without a ticket.

faqs.q: Can you walk the moat of Rhodes for free?
faqs.a: Yes. The dry moat around the medieval town is a public walk for much of its length. The walk on top of the walls is a different thing: it opens at limited times and has its own ticket.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Rhodes Old Town?
faqs.a: Half a day covers the Street of the Knights, the palace or the Archaeological Museum, the lower town and part of the moat. A full day lets you see both interiors and walk the whole moat.

faqs.q: How far is Lindos from Rhodes town?
faqs.a: About fifty kilometres down the east coast, an hour or more by bus. The Acropolis of Lindos has its own ticket, separate from anything in Rhodes town.

featured_image.alt: The walled old town of Dubrovnik and the island of Lokrum seen from Mount Srd at sunset

content_html:
[place attraction="walls-of-dubrovnik" city="dubrovnik"]

On the morning of 6 April 1667 an earthquake brought down most of Dubrovnik in a few seconds. Several thousand people died, the rector of the republic among them, and fires burned for days afterwards. The city of Gothic and Renaissance palaces was gone. The walls around it barely moved.

They were tested again in the autumn of 1991, when the Yugoslav army shelled the old town from the hills and from the sea, and more than half of its buildings were hit. That is why the roofs, seen from the top of the walls, come in two colours: the bright orange of tiles laid in the 1990s and, here and there, the paler brown of the ones that survived. The walk around the walls is the best thing to do in Dubrovnik and the most expensive. It deserves a little planning.

What the walk is

The walls form an unbroken ring of just under two kilometres, up to twenty-five metres high, built for the most part between the 14th and the 16th century. You walk on top of them, one way only, anticlockwise. There are three places to go up:

  • Pile Gate, the main entrance of the old town on the west, by a steep stair just inside the gate. It has the longest line.
  • St John's Fort, at the old port.
  • Near Ploče Gate, on the east side, by the Dominican monastery. It is usually the quietest.

Allow an hour and a half to two hours. There are many steps, no lift and almost no shade. A few kiosks on the sea side sell drinks.

The roofs from the wall walk: newer tiles in bright orange, older ones paler. Photo: Richard Mortel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What you see, in order from Pile Gate

From the Pile entrance the route turns towards the sea. You pass above Fort Bokar and follow the south wall, which rises straight out of the rocks, with the island of Lokrum offshore. At the south-east corner St John's Fort closes the old port. The route then runs above the harbour to the Ploče side and climbs along the landward wall, the thickest, to the round Minčeta Tower, finished in 1464. Its top is the highest point of the circuit, and the place from which the whole town and the main street lie below you. From there it is downhill to Pile.

The Minčeta Tower, the highest point of the circuit. Photo: Ramón, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

When to walk them

In season, be at an entrance when it opens in the morning, or go up in the last two hours before closing. Between ten and three the walkway carries the passengers of the cruise ships, and in July and August the stone gives back the heat of the sun. Late afternoon has the better light on the roofs. Check the closing hour first, because the staff clear the walls on time.

If you start at the Ploče entrance instead of Pile, you do the long climb to Minčeta at the beginning, while you are fresh, and finish along the sea. From November to March the hours are short, the walkway is nearly empty and the ticket has in past years cost less.

What the ticket covers

A ticket is one circuit of the walls. It is checked again along the way, so keep it at hand, and you cannot come down for lunch and go back up. It has long also covered Fort Lovrijenac, the fortress on a rock outside the walls to the west of Pile Gate. Its walls are about twelve metres thick towards the sea and well under one metre towards the town, so that no commander could hold it against the republic. Over its door is carved, in Latin: freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world.

The ticket does not cover the museums, the monasteries or the cable car.

Fort Lovrijenac on its rock, outside the walls to the west. Photo: Sumitsurai, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Ticket or Dubrovnik Pass

The Dubrovnik Pass is the city's card, sold for one, three or seven days. It includes the walls with Fort Lovrijenac, the main museums, among them the Rector's Palace, and the city buses. In recent seasons the one-day pass has been sold at the same price as the wall ticket on its own. If that is still so when you go, the pass is the one to buy, even for the walls alone. Compare the two before you pay, and note that the pass, like the ticket, allows a single walk around the walls.

What our partner sells: commentary, not entry

Our partner does not sell the wall ticket. What it sells in Dubrovnik are self-guided audio walks in its app, on your own phone:

  • A half-hour tour of the defences: the gates, forts and towers, from Pile Gate to the Minčeta Tower.
  • Two-hour walks of the walled town, from Pile Gate by the cathedral and the Jesuit stairs, ending at the walls or at the old port.
  • Shorter walks of the Old Town, an hour to an hour and a half along the main street, the Sponza Palace and the Rector's Palace.

None of them includes a ticket to the walls or to anything else. If you want a commentary in your ears on top of the walls, you buy the audio walk and the wall ticket separately. Bring earphones, and download the tour before you set out.

These are the audio walks our partner sells in Dubrovnik, with today's prices:

[partner city="dubrovnik" match="walls,walled" limit="6"]

What is free at street level

The old town itself costs nothing. The Stradun, the main street, runs some three hundred metres from Pile Gate to the old port, paved in limestone that centuries of feet have polished like glass. At its west end stands the large domed fountain that Onofrio della Cava built in 1438, at the end of the aqueduct. At its east end are Orlando's Column, the arcade of the Sponza Palace, the church of St Blaise and, round the corner, the cathedral. The old port and the lanes that climb in steps on both sides are free too.

The east end of the Stradun, with the arcade of the Sponza Palace on the right. Photo: Jerzy Strzelecki, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

From here

Use the same ticket for Fort Lovrijenac while it is valid. For the view from above, the cable car climbs Mount Srđ, behind the town: see our page for the Srđ cableway. Boats to Lokrum leave from the old port. Current hours for the walls of Dubrovnik are on our page. For the rest of Dubrovnik, or to fit it into a longer trip, open the trip planner for Croatia.

Cover photo: dronepicr, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

faqs.q: What is the best time to walk the Dubrovnik walls?
faqs.a: At opening time in the morning or in the last two hours before closing. Between ten and three in season the walkway is crowded with cruise passengers, and in summer it is very hot, with almost no shade.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk the walls of Dubrovnik?
faqs.a: An hour and a half to two hours for the full circuit of just under two kilometres, with stops for the views. The route is one way and has many steps.

faqs.q: Is Fort Lovrijenac included in the walls ticket?
faqs.a: The wall ticket has long also covered Fort Lovrijenac, the fortress on the rock west of Pile Gate. Check the validity printed on your ticket, and keep it after you leave the walls.

faqs.q: Is the Dubrovnik Pass worth it for the walls?
faqs.a: In recent seasons the one-day pass has cost the same as the wall ticket alone, while adding museums and buses. Compare the two prices before you buy: if they are still level, the pass is the better choice.

faqs.q: Which entrance to the Dubrovnik walls is least crowded?
faqs.a: The entrance near Ploče Gate, on the east side of the old town, is usually the quietest. The one just inside Pile Gate is the busiest.

title: Valletta on foot: a half-day route, St John's Co-Cathedral, and what is free
subtitle: A city one kilometre long, built on a grid after a siege. The stops in order, the one interior not to miss, and what costs nothing.
excerpt: A half-day walk through Valletta from City Gate to Fort St Elmo and back, with what to know before St John's Co-Cathedral, what is free, what needs a ticket and what an audio walk adds.

what is free to see in Valletta

meta_description: Valletta on foot in half a day: City Gate, the Upper Barrakka, St John's Co-Cathedral and Fort St Elmo. What is free and what needs a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The skyline of Valletta with a large dome and a church spire, seen across the water from Sliema

content_html:
[place attraction="st-john-s-co-cathedral" city="valletta"]

In May 1565 an Ottoman fleet landed an army on Malta to finish the Knights of St John, the order that Suleiman the Magnificent had driven out of Rhodes forty-three years earlier. The siege lasted nearly four months. The small fort of St Elmo, at the tip of a bare ridge between two harbours, held for a month before it fell. In September, with a relief force arriving from Sicily, the Ottomans sailed away.

The Grand Master, Jean de Valette, decided that the ridge would never be left empty again. He laid the first stone of a new city on it on 28 March 1566. The Pope lent his military engineer, Francesco Laparelli, who drew a grid of straight streets inside a ring of bastions. Valette died in 1568 and never saw it finished. The city took his name, and its plan tells you how to walk it: one main street along the spine, and side streets that fall away to the water in steps.

The route in brief

From City Gate to Fort St Elmo, along the spine, is barely one kilometre. With the two gardens and the way back it becomes a loop of three to four kilometres. Allow three hours for the streets alone and a half day with the Co-Cathedral. The main street is level. Everything to either side of it is a hill, often a staircase.

Stop by stop

1. City Gate

You enter over the old ditch through a gate redesigned by Renzo Piano, with the Parliament he built beside it. Next door stands the roofless shell of the Royal Opera House, bombed in 1942 and now used as an open-air theatre.

2. Upper Barrakka Gardens

Turn right to the highest point of the bastions. The arcaded terrace looks over the Grand Harbour to the three fortified towns opposite and to Fort St Angelo. On the level below is the Saluting Battery, whose gun is fired at midday and usually again at four. The garden and the view are free.

The Saluting Battery and the Grand Harbour from the Upper Barrakka Gardens. Photo: Anton Zelenov, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

3. Auberge de Castille

Just outside the gardens is the grandest of the inns of the knights, rebuilt in the 1740s and now the office of the Prime Minister. You see it from the square.

4. St John's Co-Cathedral

Go down Merchants Street or Republic Street to the plain, fortress-like church of the order. It has a section of its own below.

5. St George's Square and the Grandmaster's Palace

The palace of the Grand Masters, later of the British governors, fills one side of the main square. Its state rooms and armoury are visited with a ticket.

6. Fort St Elmo

The street runs downhill to the tip of the peninsula and the star-shaped fort rebuilt after the siege. It holds the National War Museum, with the George Cross awarded to the island in 1942.

7. Lower Barrakka Gardens and back

Return along the harbour side by the small Lower Barrakka Gardens, which face the harbour mouth and the Siege Bell memorial, then climb back through the side streets, under the enclosed wooden balconies that are the mark of the city.

Enclosed wooden balconies on a side street of Valletta. Photo: Godwin Borg, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

St John's Co-Cathedral: what to know before you go in

Girolamo Cassar built it between 1573 and 1578 as the church of the order, with a front as bare as a barracks. The inside is the opposite. In the 1660s the painter Mattia Preti had every wall carved and gilded and painted the vault with the life of St John. The floor is made of some four hundred inlaid marble tombstones of knights. Each of the side chapels belonged to one of the national groups of the order.

In the Oratory hangs The Beheading of St John the Baptist, which Caravaggio painted in 1608. It is the largest canvas he made and the only one he signed, in the blood that runs from the saint's neck. He painted it as a newly made knight. Before the year was out he had been jailed after a brawl, had escaped from the island, and was expelled from the order in his absence, in that same room, in front of his own painting.

The "Co" dates from 1816, when the church was given equal rank with the older cathedral in Mdina.

Visitors enter with a ticket, which has long included an audio guide. The church has for years been closed to visitors on Sundays and public holidays, with a shorter day on Saturday. Shoulders and knees must be covered, and narrow high heels are not allowed on the marble floor. Allow an hour to an hour and a half. Current hours are on our page for St John's Co-Cathedral.

Inside the Co-Cathedral: no surface was left plain. Photo: Simon Burchell, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free and what needs a ticket

Free: the streets and stairs, City Gate, both Barrakka gardens, the squares, and the view down onto the Saluting Battery.

Ticketed: the Co-Cathedral, the Grandmaster's Palace, Fort St Elmo with the War Museum, the terrace of the Saluting Battery itself, and the National Museum of Archaeology on Republic Street, which keeps the small prehistoric figure known as the Sleeping Lady.

Audio walks: what our partner sells

Our partner sells no entry tickets in Valletta. It sells self-guided audio walks: you download one in the partner's app, and your phone tells the stories from stop to stop, with a map. They last two to three hours and differ mainly in where they begin:

  • one runs the length of the city from City Gate to Fort St Elmo;
  • one starts at the Upper Barrakka Gardens and ends in St George's Square;
  • one starts at the ruins of the opera house and ends in the same square;
  • one starts at Fort St Elmo and works back through the city.

All of them stop outside the Co-Cathedral. None includes its ticket, or any other. Bring earphones.

These are the audio walks our partner sells in Valletta, with today's prices:

[partner city="valletta" match="valletta" limit="4"]

From here

A lift beside the Upper Barrakka Gardens goes down to the waterfront, where a small ferry crosses the Grand Harbour to the three towns you looked at from the terrace. On the other side of the peninsula another ferry crosses to Sliema, which has the best view back at the skyline. For the rest of Valletta and the island, open the trip planner for Malta.

Cover photo: Keith Ruffles, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

faqs.q: Can you see Valletta in half a day on foot?
faqs.a: Yes. The city is about one kilometre long. A loop from City Gate by the Upper Barrakka Gardens, St John's Co-Cathedral, the palace square and Fort St Elmo takes three hours on the street, or a half day with the Co-Cathedral.

faqs.q: Do you need a ticket for St John's Co-Cathedral?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors enter with a ticket, which has long included an audio guide. The church has for years been closed to visitors on Sundays and public holidays, so check the current hours before you go.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Valletta?
faqs.a: The streets, City Gate, the Upper and Lower Barrakka Gardens with their views of the Grand Harbour, and the squares. The Co-Cathedral, the palace, Fort St Elmo and the museums need tickets.

faqs.q: What time do the cannons fire in Valletta?
faqs.a: The gun of the Saluting Battery, below the Upper Barrakka Gardens, is fired at midday and usually again at four in the afternoon. You can watch from the garden terrace for free.

faqs.q: Where is Caravaggio's painting in Malta?
faqs.a: The Beheading of St John the Baptist, painted in 1608, hangs in the Oratory of St John's Co-Cathedral in Valletta. It is seen with the ticket to the church.
